forks.actual: General Foods expanded Burger Chef and Rix to 1,200 outlets within about three years of buying roughly 700, then closed more than 100 and planned to cut a quarter of the chain.[^1]
forks.whatif: The founders had added several hundred restaurants in a decade, with new franchisees sent to Indianapolis for training.[^4][^5] Holding to that pace would have left a smaller chain in 1972, but one without the write-down, and with the capital that went into bad sites still available for the good ones.

forks.actual: The founder left after the sale, and within two years almost the whole management had changed. A General Foods executive later conceded that fast food was “not like manufacturing a pound of coffee.”[^1]
forks.whatif: An earn-out for the founders, or a separate restaurant management of the kind Pillsbury set up at Burger King when it hired Donald Smith in 1977 to restructure the franchise system[^21], might have kept site selection and franchise relations in experienced hands during the expansion.

forks.actual: General Foods kept the chain for another ten years after the write-off, shrinking it to a regional business that was barely breaking even by 1981, and sold it for about $44 million.[^2][^3]
forks.whatif: A sale to a restaurant operator in 1972, while the chain still had more than 1,000 units and the second-largest footprint in the industry, might have preserved the name. Whether any buyer existed at a price General Foods would accept is unknown.
